messages.subject: Strange behaviour: "i" as data GOOD; "i" as parameter PREDICTED WELL but rest NOT converge
parts:
Hello Community,

my model (attached) tries to find regression with a variable gamma loss function.

If I give the "i" (-2.302585) as data all good.


fit <- rstan:::stan(

  model_file="regression_works.stan", 

  data = list(N=length(y), x=t(log(x)), x2=t(log(x)^2), y = log(y), P=1, P_real=1, prob=p, mode= median(x2), i=-log(p))

)


traceplot(

  fit, 

  pars =                       c("a1", "a2", "b1", "b2", "b3"), 

  inc_warmup =                 TRUE

)



If I try to calculate "i" it has problem to converge, although the prediction should be straightforward

fit <- rstan:::stan(

  model_file="regression_NOT_works.stan", 

  data = list(N=length(y), x=t(log(x)), x2=t(log(x)^2), y = log(y), P=1, P_real=1, prob=p, mode= median(x2), i=-log(p))

)


traceplot(

  fit, 

  pars =                       c("a1", "a2", "b1", "b2", "b3", "i"), 

  inc_warmup =                 TRUE

)




When the prediction is easier, "i" converge immediately, but all the rest of parameters do not!



Somebody has some clues?


Thanks!

I'm afraid I don't undertand the model and the constraints
on the variables. It looks like this is introducing double
noise terms:

i ~ gamma(i_alpha, (i_alpha-1)/-log(1/(P_real+1))); //mode at 0.7

target += gamma_lpdf(y - (x[1] - i) | alpha,beta);

understand the model.

For gamma distributions, you might want to put priors on the
alpha and beta, as well, especially as you have one for
each of the observations.

A typical univariate linear regression would be of the form

and y is then modeled using x. There's a chapter in the manual
that goes over basic measurement error models in the predictors.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Strange behaviour: "i" as data GOOD; "i" as parameter PREDICTED WELL but rest NOT converge
parts:
OK. I was just thrown off by the form of your regression, which is
just a hardcoded slope of 1 and intercept of i (we like to use Greek
letters for parameters and reserve variables like i, j, k, and m, n for
integers). And it doesn't roll the mean into the (alpha, beta) terms (or
does it?) in
target += gamma_lpdf(y - (x[1] - i) | alpha,beta);

as you usually see in a standard GLM.

In order to have a positive variate for the gamma distribution, you
need

y - x[1] + i > 0,

or equivalently

i > x[1] - y,

which means you need a lower bound for i of

max(x[1] - y) == max(x[1]) - y

I don't understand the rest of the regression, but that's
probably not important.

And forget what I said about priors on alpha and beta;
I hadn't kept in mind they are transformed parameters and you
do have priors on the components.

- Bob

P.S. It's easier for us with just text for the models and GIF/JPG for
images.
